Heaton Camp mileage in approach prose

before.approach: McGregor Mountain is only reachable via Stehekin, at the head of Lake Chelan, which has no outside road access — get there by the Lady of the Lake ferry, floatplane, or the long trail from Cascade Pass/Bridge Creek. From Stehekin Landing, take the NPS shuttle bus (or walk/bike) 11 miles up the Stehekin Valley Road to its end at High Bridge (a hiking permit is required for the overnight version of this trip). From High Bridge, follow the Old Wagon Road/PCT north; at about 1.3 miles reach the signed junction where the McGregor Mountain Trail forks right and climbs past Coon Lake toward Howard Lake — Howard Lake is a reliable water source and a good gut-check that you're on route. Beyond the lake the trail switchbacks relentlessly (climbers report close to 100 switchbacks) up through forest and rocky slopes that get hot and dry with little shade or water, gaining roughly 6,500 ft over the next 5.5-6 miles to Heaton Camp at about 7,000 ft (mile 7 of 7.7), a small single-party designated site where a seasonal-snowmelt stream just below camp is the last dependable water before the summit push. From Heaton Camp the maintained trail continues another quarter- to half-mile to where it ends at the base of a talus field; total stats to the true summit are 7.7 miles and 6,600 ft one-way. The final roughly 1,000-1,100 vertical feet is an exposed Class 2-3 scramble, not a trail: intermittent (and often faded) red arrows painted on the rock mark the line, which loops right then left behind a lower sub-summit, crosses a snowfield/talus shelf above the Sandalee Glacier, then follows a fairly level shoulder past an old radio installation to the true summit and former fire-lookout site. Carry an ice axe if snow still covers the talus or the glacier traverse (common into midsummer), and expect loose rock ('kitty litter' on slabs) and real exposure on the ledges near the top — staying precisely on the arrow-marked line matters, as it gets noticeably dicier off-route.

fitnessSpec.hiking: Very strong - the trail alone is ~7.5 miles one-way with roughly 5,700-6,700 ft of gain to its end, plus additional scrambling and elevation to the summit; most parties do this as an overnight rather than a huge single-push day
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Overnight pack (30-40+ lb) is typical since most parties camp near Heaton Camp given the remote, self-rescue-only access; a very fit team could attempt a light/fast single-push day

partner_requirements.approachTime: Full day to reach the scramble start (6.5-7.5 mi, ~5,700-6,700 ft gain to trail's end/Heaton Camp); most parties treat this as a multi-day trip rather than a single push
requiredSkills: confident Class 3 scrambling on loose, exposed rock
route-finding above the trail's end (talus field then ledgy rock marked by old paint/arrows in places)
sound judgment managing exposure without a rope, or willingness to carry/place protection for the final block
self-rescue mindset - evacuation from this area is slow and remote
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Experienced scrambler comfortable with sustained, loose Class 3 terrain and real exposure; several trip reports and NPS notes suggest a rope is advisable for the final summit block even though it's graded Class 3

waypoints.name: High Bridge Trailhead
waypoints.note: Reached via NPS shuttle from Stehekin Landing (11 mi up-valley); no facilities at trailhead, backcountry permit required for overnight stays at the Golden West Visitor Center.

waypoints.name: Howard Lake junction
waypoints.note: Trail passes Howard Lake then reaches a signed junction where the McGregor Mountain Trail splits off from the Howard Lake/PCT connector.
waypoints.directions: From High Bridge follow the Old Wagon Road and PCT north; the tread climbs steadily, passes Coon Lake and reaches Howard Lake. The signed McGregor Mountain junction is a short way past the lake, just before the PCT tips over and starts back downhill, so if you are losing elevation you have gone too far. Howard Lake is reliable water and a useful confirmation you are on route.

waypoints.name: 2.9-mile viewpoint and falls
waypoints.note: Valley viewpoint after the first sustained climb (2,100 ft gained from the trailhead); a short scramble path drops to a seasonal falls for water.
waypoints.directions: Turn off the PCT onto the McGregor Mountain Trail. It winds around and behind the lake, then commits to one long switchback across a hot, dusty open slope before settling into the grind. Roughly 2,100 ft of climbing brings you out at a valley viewpoint, where a short scramble path drops to a seasonal falls; it is worth the detour, because shade and water are both scarce from here on.

waypoints.name: Heaton Camp
waypoints.note: Only established campsite on the mountain, in subalpine forest just below treeline; single-party site, water from a seasonal snowmelt stream a short distance below camp on the trail.
waypoints.directions: This is the long stretch: close to a hundred switchbacks up an open southwest-facing shoulder that bakes in the afternoon, then into stunted subalpine fir and pine. The trail crosses a clear creek and reaches the lower of two glacial cirques on rocky, sandy moraine, with the camp just above the terminal moraine among larches. Start early, because there is essentially no shade and no dependable water until the seasonal snowmelt stream just below camp.

waypoints.name: Trail end / base of summit scramble
waypoints.note: Maintained tread ends here on the high shoulder below the summit block; route-finding begins across talus toward the base of the scree slope.
waypoints.directions: Above camp the tread throws another set of tight switchbacks at you and ends in about a third of a mile at a rocky outcropping. There is no maintained trail past this point. Talus leads on toward the base of the summit block, and the route-finding starts here.

waypoints.name: Summit block scramble ledges
waypoints.note: Class 3 hand-and-foot scramble up loose talus and exposed rock ledges to a notch left of the true summit, marked only by faint, intermittent red-painted arrows; carry an ice axe if snow lingers.
waypoints.directions: The last 1,000-1,100 ft is exposed class 2-3 scrambling on loose rock, marked only by faded red arrows painted on the rock: the line loops right, then back left behind a lower sub-summit, then crosses a snowfield and talus shelf above the Sandalee Glacier. Staying precisely on the arrows matters, because the ground gets noticeably worse off-route and gravelly slab sits directly above serious exposure. Carry an ice axe if snow still covers the talus or the shelf, which is common into midsummer, and a helmet is worth it on this section.

waypoints.name: McGregor Mountain summit
waypoints.note: True summit gained from the backside through the notch; views of Bonanza, Glacier, and Dome peaks and the Stehekin valley.
waypoints.directions: From the top of the ledges the ground levels onto a shoulder running past an old radio installation to the true summit and former lookout site, gained from the back through a notch beside the high point. Downclimbing this scramble is the more dangerous half of the day, so fix the line in your head on the way up rather than working it out again from above.

approach_variants.name: High Bridge and the McGregor Mountain Trail
approach_variants.notes: There is no road to the bottom of this one — Stehekin is reached by boat, floatplane or the long trail in, and from Stehekin Landing the valley road runs eleven miles up to its end at High Bridge, walkable, bikeable or by shuttle. From High Bridge the tread heads north on the old wagon grade and the Pacific Crest Trail, climbs steadily past Coon Lake to Howard Lake, and reaches the signed McGregor Mountain junction a short way past the lake, just before the crest trail tips over and starts back downhill. Howard Lake is reliable water and a useful confirmation you are on route; if you are losing elevation you have walked past the junction. Above the junction the trail winds behind the lake, commits to one long switchback across a hot, dusty open slope, and then settles into a relentless grind — close to a hundred switchbacks up an open southwest-facing shoulder with essentially no shade. A seasonal falls off a short scramble path near the first big viewpoint is worth the detour, because water is scarce from there on. The trail crosses a clear creek, reaches the lower of two glacial cirques on rocky, sandy moraine, and ends at Heaton Camp just above the terminal moraine among larches, where a snowmelt stream a short way below camp is the last dependable water. Above camp another set of tight switchbacks ends at a rocky outcropping and the maintained trail simply stops.
approach_variants.season: August into early September is the reliable window, once the talus and the shelf above the glacier have melted out. Carry an axe if snow still lies on either.
hazards: roughly a vertical mile of gain from the valley floor with almost no shade and no dependable water below Heaton Camp
loose gravel on slab directly above significant exposure on the summit ledges — the descent is the more dangerous half
route-finding, not climbing difficulty, is the real crux above the trail's end
a snowfield and talus shelf above the Sandalee Glacier that can hold firm snow into midsummer
no road access to the trailhead itself, so an injured party is a long way from help
approach_variants.baseFinding: A PAINTED RED ARROW ON ONE LARGE BOULDER IS THE PROOF. Where the maintained tread ends at the rocky outcropping above Heaton Camp, talus leads on toward the summit block. Out in the middle of that boulder field, one large rock carries a big bright red arrow painted on it pointing uphill, and from that rock more arrows are visible above it in a chain running up the ledges. Find that first arrow before you commit to any line. The marked route loops right, then back left behind a lower sub-summit, crosses a snowfield and talus shelf above the Sandalee Glacier, and finishes along a fairly level shoulder past an old radio installation to the true summit, where a park radio repeater now stands on the site of the old lookout. If you are working up talus and cannot see a painted arrow anywhere above you, you have not found the route yet — do not improvise a line, because the ground gets noticeably worse off the arrows and gravelly slab sits directly above serious drops. A second check: on the marked line there are no climbing moves, only the occasional handhold for balance on a narrow ledge. If you are pulling on rock to make upward progress, you are off the arrows.

climbing_route.label: Arrow-marked scramble behind the sub-summit
climbing_route.notes: The final roughly 1,000-1,100 vertical feet is an exposed scramble, not a trail. Intermittent and often faded red arrows painted on the rock mark the line, which loops right then left behind a lower sub-summit. Expect loose rock ('kitty litter' on slabs) — staying precisely on the arrow-marked line matters, as it gets noticeably dicier off-route.

climbing_route.label: Snowfield/talus shelf above the Sandalee Glacier
climbing_route.notes: The line crosses a snowfield/talus shelf above the Sandalee Glacier; carry an ice axe if snow still covers the talus or the glacier traverse, common into midsummer.

climbing_route.label: Summit shoulder
climbing_route.notes: A fairly level shoulder past an old radio installation leads to the true summit and former fire-lookout site. Real exposure on the ledges near the top.

before.permit: No climbing or wilderness permit required; Northwest Forest Pass (or day fee) to park at developed trailheads.

access.fees: NPS valley shuttle bus, High Bridge to/from Stehekin Landing: $10/adult, $5/child one-way (peak-season rate); Lady of the Lake round-trip ferry from Chelan or Field's Point: roughly $40.50/adult
access.notes: This corridor is inside the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area (North Cascades National Park Service Complex). No Mount Rainier-style climbing fee applies here.
access.rules: Pets and hunting prohibited in this NPS unit; hiker and stock use permitted on the trail
access.permit: Free NPS backcountry permit required for any overnight stay (e.g. Heaton Camp, a single-party site for up to 12 people/stock at 7,000 ft); walk-up permits are issued at the Golden West Visitor Center in Stehekin, or reserved ahead for $20 plus a non-refundable $6 fee
access.closures: Sisi Fire: North Cascades National Park's Sisi Fire closures (its fire-closure list, updated September 14, 2026, gives no end date) close the McGregor Mountain Trail, Heaton Camp, High Bridge Camp, the High Bridge area and the Stehekin Valley Road from Stehekin Valley Ranch to High Bridge. This route cannot be approached while those closures stand. North Cascades National Park: (360) 854-7200.
access.seasonal: WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) closes gate-to-gate roughly early December–mid/late April; the entire Washington Pass corridor is car-inaccessible in winter.
access.landManager: Lake Chelan National Recreation Area (North Cascades NP complex)
access.land_manager: Lake Chelan National Recreation Area (North Cascades National Park Service Complex)
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Washington Pass Overlook, Blue Lake, and Cutthroat trailheads — $5/day or $30/annual (America the Beautiful pass also honored).

overnight_permit.what: North Cascades National Park Service Complex backcountry permit, fee charged
overnight_permit.where: Reserve on Recreation.gov, or arrange it with the park the day before you travel; there is no permit office or cell service in Stehekin.

itinerary.cal: The ferry (Lady of the Lake) runs once daily to Stehekin and the scramble is typically snow-free only from mid/late summer into early fall, so most trips require a Stehekin overnight before and/or after; a free backcountry permit for Heaton Camp is required from the Golden West Visitor Center.

days.note: From the High Bridge trailhead (reached via the Lady of the Lake ferry to Stehekin and the NPS shuttle), follow the PCT north to Howard Lake, then turn onto the McGregor Mountain Trail and grind up roughly 100 switchbacks through forest and into larches. Camp and get water at Heaton Camp (~6,700 ft), the only established site on the mountain; a free NPS backcountry permit (Golden West Visitor Center) is required.
days.title: Approach to Heaton Camp
days.objective: Backpack from High Bridge trailhead to Heaton Camp

days.note: Leave camp early with a light pack (helmet, light rope/harness optional) for the final quarter-to-half mile of exposed, technical scrambling above the Sandalee Glacier snowfield, following faded red arrows and cairns to the summit block. Return to camp, break it down, and hike the full ~6.8 miles back out to High Bridge with a full pack in time to catch the shuttle/ferry.
days.title: Summit scramble and hike out

schedule.label: Leave Heaton Camp
schedule.detail: Light day pack for the scramble; full packs and camp gear left behind for now.

schedule.label: Reach base of summit block
schedule.detail: Talus slope gives way to steep, exposed rock scrambling marked by red arrows.

schedule.label: Summit (8,143 ft)
schedule.detail: Sweeping views of the Stehekin Valley, Lake Chelan, and the North Cascades.

schedule.label: Back at Heaton Camp
schedule.detail: Break camp, refill water, eat, and repack for the hike out.

schedule.label: Begin hike out
schedule.detail: Full pack, ~5,100 ft of descent over ~6.8 miles back to High Bridge.

schedule.label: Reach High Bridge trailhead
schedule.detail: Catch the NPS shuttle back to Stehekin Landing for the return ferry.

days.objective: Scramble the summit block, then break camp and hike all the way out to High Bridge

itinerary.totalNote: A ~15-mile round trip with about 6,600 ft of gain to the true summit; most parties backpack in to Heaton Camp and treat the exposed, rope-suggested summit scramble plus the full hike out as one long second day, though very fit trail runners do the whole thing car-to-car in a single 10-14 hr push.

before.rope_note: The final ~1-mile summit scramble above the maintained Stehekin-side trail climbs loose Class 3 rock marked by faded red/orange arrows, passing through a notch left of the summit. Parties describe serious exposure in several places — a short handline is prudent for less-experienced parties, though most scramblers go unroped.

July.reason: Primary scramble window - snow largely cleared from the summit block while trail/water access is generally reliable

June.reason: High terrain and the summit block area typically still hold snow this early; snowbound high terrain into summer

August.reason: Driest, most stable east-side conditions of the season; best combination of snow-free rock and settled weather

October.reason: Outside the best-season window; early snow and short daylight make the long approach and exposed summit block considerably more hazardous

September.reason: Clear, dry east-side conditions typical of fall, but shorter days and possible early-season snow at elevation reduce the margin
